<meta>Text D3862 in the Derge Tengyur catalogue numbering. This is the opening of Candrakīrti's autocommentary on his Madhyamakāvatāra. The "#" marks in the transcription appear to be line or layout markers and are not rendered.</meta>

In the language of India: *Madhyamakāvatārabhāṣyanāma*. In the language of Tibet: *An Explanation of "Entering the Middle Way"*.

Homage to the noble Mañjuśrī, the ever-youthful!

In order to enter into the treatises of the Middle Way <note>original: "dbu ma'i bstan bcos," that is, the Madhyamaka treatises of Nāgārjuna</note>, the author wishes to compose *Entering the Middle Way*. To show that the Blessed One, great compassion, is worthy of praise at the very outset, even by the perfectly complete Buddhas and the bodhisattvas, he composes two verses. Great compassion is the first and excellent cause of buddhahood itself, and its defining character is to protect, without exception, the countless beings who are bound in the prison of cyclic existence and have no refuge. The verses begin:

*Śrāvakas and middling buddhas are born from the Lords of Sages;*
*Buddhas are born from bodhisattvas;*
*And the mind of compassion, nondual understanding,*
*And the mind of awakening are the causes of the children of the Victors.*

<note>The "middling buddhas" are the pratyekabuddhas, or solitary realizers, placed between the śrāvakas and the fully awakened Buddhas.</note>

Here, the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, are called "Lords of Sages" <term>thub dbang</term> <gloss>Munīndra, lord among sages</gloss> because they possess the unsurpassed and excellent sovereignty over the Dharma, an excellent supreme lordship greater even than that of the śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas and bodhisattvas, and because the śrāvakas and the others are governed by their word. That the śrāvakas and the others are "born" from them means that they are brought forth by them.

How is this so? When Buddhas have appeared, they engage in teaching dependent origination without error. Then, through the stages of hearing, reflecting on and meditating on that teaching, the śrāvakas and the others are brought to completion, each in accordance with their particular inclination.

Suppose that some, though they have become skilled in realizing the ultimate merely by hearing the teaching of dependent origination, do not attain nirvāṇa in this very life in which they see the truth. Even so, just as the fruit of an action is certain to ripen, those who practise what was taught will fully obtain the fruit they aspire to in another life

<summary>This is the opening of Candrakīrti's own commentary on his *Entering the Middle Way*. It gives the title, pays homage to Mañjuśrī, and begins explaining the first verse: śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas are "born from the Lords of Sages" because they reach their goal by hearing and practising the Buddhas' teaching of dependent origination.</summary>
<keywords>Candrakīrti, Madhyamakāvatārabhāṣya, Entering the Middle Way, Madhyamaka, Mañjuśrī, great compassion, Lord of Sages, Munīndra, śrāvaka, pratyekabuddha, bodhisattva, dependent origination, nirvāṇa, Derge Tengyur, D3862</keywords>

<meta>continues from previous page: the fruit "will fully..."</meta>ripen, and they will obtain it without fail. As the noble Āryadeva has said:

*Even if one who knows reality*
*Does not attain nirvāṇa here,*
*In another birth, without effort,*
*He will surely attain it, just as with karma.*

For this very reason it is also said in the *Middle Way* <note>Nāgārjuna's *Mūlamadhyamakakārikā*, the root treatise of the Madhyamaka school</note>:

*When perfect Buddhas do not appear,*
*And the śrāvakas too have passed away,*
*The wisdom of the solitary buddhas*
*Arises fully, without reliance.*

Now, they are called *śrāvakas* <term>nyan thos</term> <gloss>hearers</gloss> because they obtain the fruit of correct instruction by hearing it, and then declare, "Thus has what was to be done been done. I know no other existence beyond this one," and so on. <note>This is the traditional declaration of an arhat who has reached liberation.</note>

Alternatively, they are called *śrāvakas*, "those who cause to hear," because, having heard from the Tathāgatas the supreme fruit, the path of unsurpassed, perfectly complete buddhahood, they proclaim it to those who seek it. As it is said in the *Sūtra of the White Lotus of the Holy Dharma* <note>the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*, or Lotus Sūtra</note>:

*Protector, today we have become hearers;*
*We shall rightly proclaim supreme awakening,*
*And we shall fully utter the word "awakening."*
*Therefore we are like hearers who are never exhausted.*

Bodhisattvas, too, do this. Even so, it does not follow that bodhisattvas are śrāvakas, for the śrāvakas are those who merely proclaim it, but do not themselves accomplish even something in accord with it.

This word "buddha" applies to all three: śrāvakas, solitary buddhas, and unsurpassed, perfectly complete Buddhas. Therefore the solitary buddhas are designated by the word "buddha." They are "middling" because, through the distinction of their greater increase in merit and wisdom, they are superior to the śrāvakas; and because they lack the accumulations of merit and wisdom, great compassion, omniscience and the like, they are inferior to the perfectly complete Buddhas. For this very reason, because their wisdom arises without being taught, and because they are solitary, they are called self-

<summary>Candrakīrti cites Āryadeva and Nāgārjuna to show that hearing the teaching of dependent origination bears fruit even in a later life. He then explains two meanings of the word *śrāvaka*, "hearer," and why the pratyekabuddhas are called "middling buddhas," ranking above the śrāvakas but below the fully awakened Buddhas.</summary>
<keywords>Candrakīrti, Madhyamakāvatārabhāṣya, Āryadeva, Nāgārjuna, Mūlamadhyamakakārikā, Lotus Sūtra, śrāvaka, pratyekabuddha, solitary buddha, nirvāṇa, dependent origination, Madhyamaka, Derge Tengyur</keywords>

<meta>continues from previous page: "self-buddhas," i.e. pratyekabuddhas</meta>awakened, they are "self-buddhas" <term>rang sangs rgyas</term> <gloss>pratyekabuddhas, solitary realizers</gloss>.

In the way just explained, the śrāvakas and the solitary buddhas come forth definitively from the Dharma taught by the Tathāgatas, and therefore they are "born from the Lords of Sages."

Then from whom are those Lords of Sages themselves born? To answer this he says: *Buddhas are born from bodhisattvas.*

Objection: Are not the bodhisattvas also called "children of the Victor" because they are born from the teaching of the Tathāgatas? How, then, can the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, be born from bodhisattvas?

Reply: This is true. Nevertheless, bodhisattvas become the cause of the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, for two reasons: because of the distinction of stages, and because they cause others to take up the mind of awakening.

As to the distinction of stages: the stage of a Tathāgata has the stage of a bodhisattva as its cause.

As to causing others to take up the mind of awakening: it is held, for example, that the noble Mañjuśrī, while he was a bodhisattva, caused the Blessed One Śākyamuni and other Tathāgatas, at the very beginning, to take up the mind of awakening.

Therefore, with regard to the principal cause of that ultimate fruit, it is taught that the Tathāgatas are born from bodhisattvas.

For this very reason, because an excellent cause is the weightiest thing, and intending that praise of the cause implicitly carries with it praise of the fruit, the author wishes to show the following. Those Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, are like a great medicinal tree that gives countless certain fruits; the bodhisattva, who is like that tree in its early stage as a sprout and so on, with tender young leaves, must be carefully and thoroughly protected. And in order that the mass of beings who are near at that time, and who are placed in the three vehicles, may be definitively joined to the Great Vehicle alone, the bodhisattva

<summary>Candrakīrti explains why the Buddhas are said to be "born from bodhisattvas": the bodhisattva stage is the cause of buddhahood, and bodhisattvas such as Mañjuśrī first inspired future Buddhas to take up the mind of awakening. He compares the bodhisattva to the young sprout of a great medicinal tree that must be protected.</summary>
<keywords>Candrakīrti, Madhyamakāvatārabhāṣya, bodhisattva, Buddha, pratyekabuddha, śrāvaka, Mañjuśrī, Śākyamuni, mind of awakening, bodhicitta, three vehicles, Great Vehicle, Mahāyāna, medicinal tree, cause and fruit</keywords>

<meta>continues from previous page: "the bodhisattva..." The author's purpose in praising bodhisattvas is being explained.</meta>he offers praise to the bodhisattvas. As it is said in the noble *Heap of Jewels Sūtra* <note>the *Ratnakūṭa* collection</note>:

"Kāśyapa, it is like this: people bow to the new moon, not to the full moon. Kāśyapa, in the same way, those who have deep faith in me should bow to the bodhisattvas, and not so to the Tathāgatas. Why is that? Because the Tathāgatas arise from the bodhisattvas, and all the śrāvakas and solitary buddhas arise from the Tathāgatas."

Thus, by reasoning and by scripture, it has been established that the Tathāgatas are born from bodhisattvas.

Then what is the cause of these bodhisattvas? To answer this he says:

*And the mind of compassion, nondual understanding,*
*And the mind of awakening are the causes of the children of the Victors.*

Here, compassion is loving tenderness; its aspects and its own nature will be explained later in this very text. Nondual understanding is the wisdom free from the two extremes, such as existence and non-existence.

As for the mind of awakening, the noble *Sūtra That Discusses All Dharmas* <note>Tibetan "chos kun bgro ba'i mdo," possibly the *Sarvadharmapravṛttinirdeśa*</note> says:

"A bodhisattva comes to understand all phenomena through the mind of awakening. All phenomena are equal to the sphere of reality. All phenomena are adventitious and do not abide; they are merely to be known, and because they are empty of a knower, they are merely to be fully understood. Thinking, 'Beings should come to understand this very nature of things,' whatever mind arises in the bodhisattva is called the bodhisattva's mind of awakening.

It is a mind of benefit and happiness toward all beings; an unsurpassed mind; a mind made gentle by love; a mind that compassion does not let turn back; a mind without regret, through joy; a mind without stain, through equanimity;

<summary>Candrakīrti quotes the *Ratnakūṭa* comparison of bodhisattvas to the new moon, which people honour more than the full moon, and so confirms that Buddhas arise from bodhisattvas. He then begins to define the three causes of bodhisattvas: compassion, nondual understanding, and the mind of awakening, quoting a sūtra on the qualities of the awakened mind.</summary>
<keywords>Candrakīrti, Madhyamakāvatārabhāṣya, Ratnakūṭa, Kāśyapa, new moon, full moon, bodhisattva, Tathāgata, compassion, nondual understanding, two extremes, mind of awakening, bodhicitta, sphere of reality, dharmadhātu, love, joy, equanimity</keywords>

<meta>continues from previous page: the sūtra's list of the qualities of the mind of awakening</meta>a mind that does not change, through emptiness; a mind without obscuration, because it is without signs; and a mind that does not abide, because it is without wishes." So it is taught. <note>Emptiness, signlessness and wishlessness are the "three doors of liberation" in Buddhist teaching.</note>

The principal causes of bodhisattvas are these three qualities: compassion, nondual wisdom, and the mind of awakening. As it is said in the *Precious Garland* <note>the *Ratnāvalī* of Nāgārjuna</note>:

*Its root is the mind of awakening,*
*Steady like the king of mountains;*
*Compassion that reaches to the ends of every direction;*
*And wisdom that does not rely on duality.*

Since compassion is also the root of both the mind of awakening and nondual wisdom, the author wishes to show that compassion is the most important, and so he says:

*Because love alone is held to be like the seed of the excellent harvest of the Victors,*
*Like water for its increase, and like its ripening*
*Into a state to be enjoyed for a long time,*
*Therefore I shall first praise compassion.*

Just as for an excellent outer crop, such as grain, the seed, the water and the ripening are most important and indispensable at the beginning, the middle and the end, so compassion alone is shown to be indispensable at all three times for the excellent harvest of the Victors.

For one who has compassion suffers at the suffering of others. In order to protect every suffering being without exception, he therefore firmly generates the resolve: "Without fail, I shall draw this whole world out of suffering and definitively join it to buddhahood." And because this pledge cannot be fulfilled if nondual wisdom is abandoned, he also enters into nondual wisdom with certainty. Therefore compassion alone is the seed of all the qualities of a Buddha. As it is said in the *Precious Garland*:

*The Great Vehicle, in which all conduct*
*Is preceded by compassion,*
*And stainless wisdom is taught:*
*What thinking person would disparage it?*

<summary>Candrakīrti completes the sūtra quotation on the mind of awakening and names compassion, nondual wisdom and the mind of awakening as the three causes of bodhisattvas. He then explains why compassion comes first: like seed, water and ripening for a crop, it is needed at the beginning, middle and end of the path to buddhahood.</summary>
<keywords>Candrakīrti, Madhyamakāvatārabhāṣya, Nāgārjuna, Ratnāvalī, Precious Garland, compassion, love, nondual wisdom, mind of awakening, bodhicitta, emptiness, signlessness, wishlessness, harvest metaphor, seed, Great Vehicle, Mahāyāna</keywords>

<meta>continues from previous page: explanation of compassion as seed, water and ripening; this sentence begins "Even when the mind of awakening has been generated..."</meta>Even when the mind of awakening has been generated, if afterwards it is not moistened again and again by the water of compassion, then, without having gathered the vast mass of fruit, it will certainly pass into nirvāṇa through the final nirvāṇa of the śrāvakas and solitary buddhas.

Even when the stage of limitless fruit has been reached, if afterwards it becomes separated from the ripening of compassion, it will not be enjoyed for a long time, and the great mass of noble fruit will not keep increasing for a long time in an unbroken succession, passed on from one to the next.

Now, wishing to make clear the distinctive nature of compassion according to the different objects on which it focuses, and to pay homage to it, he says:

*First thinking "I," they cling to a self;*
*Thinking "this is mine," they grow attached to things.*
*To that compassion for beings who, like a waterwheel's buckets, are powerless,*
*I bow down.*

Before it clings to things as "mine," this world, through the grasping at "I," imagines that a self exists that does not exist, and clings to it as true. Then it clings to every kind of thing other than the object of that "I"-grasping, thinking, "This is mine."

This world, which clings to "I" and "mine," is like a waterwheel. It is bound very tightly by the ropes of karma and the afflictions. It moves in dependence on consciousness, which drives it like the operator who turns the machine. It swings without pause through the great, deep well of cyclic existence, from the Peak of Existence down to the Avīci hell <note>the highest heaven of the formless realm and the lowest of the hells, the two limits of saṃsāra</note>. It goes downward by itself, of its own accord, and is drawn up only with great effort. Although it has the three kinds of affliction, namely the afflictions such as ignorance, karma, and birth, no fixed order of first, last and middle can be found among them. Every day it is battered by the suffering of suffering and the suffering of change. Thus it remains, never passing beyond the condition of a waterwheel's bucket. To whom

<summary>Candrakīrti finishes explaining compassion as the water and ripening of the Buddha's harvest, then introduces the verse of homage to compassion for beings. He develops the famous image of beings as the buckets of a waterwheel, bound by karma and afflictions and endlessly rising and falling through saṃsāra.</summary>
<keywords>Candrakīrti, Madhyamakāvatārabhāṣya, compassion, mind of awakening, self-grasping, "I" and "mine", waterwheel, saṃsāra, karma, afflictions, ignorance, Peak of Existence, Avīci hell, suffering of change, suffering of suffering, nirvāṇa</keywords>

<meta>continues from previous page: "To whom..." The phrase "the nectar of the Dharma ... all wrong conceptions" appears twice in the transcription, the first time out of place after "ignorance"; it seems to be a scribal anticipation of the later phrase and is rendered literally where it stands.</meta>
the bodhisattva, suffering at the suffering of those beings, focuses on them with intense compassion and is eager to protect them. For that reason, at the very beginning, I bow deeply to the Blessed Mother, Great Compassion. This is the compassion of bodhisattvas that focuses on beings.

To make clear, by way of its object, the compassion that focuses on phenomena and the compassion without an object as well, he says:

*Seeing beings as moving and as empty of their own nature,*
*Like the moon in rippling water...*

This is to be joined with *"To that compassion ... I bow down."*

When very clear water, stirred by a wind that is not too strong, is covered here and there with ripples, the reflection of the moon appears in it, together with the moon itself which was seen before as its support, as if the things that perish along with it were directly perceived. Then the wise see these two as standing there as though making plain their own nature: namely, impermanence at every moment, and emptiness of inherent nature.

In the same way, bodhisattvas who are under the sway of compassion see beings in the lake of the view of the perishing aggregates <note>the view that the transitory body and mind are a real self</note>, of ignorance, the cause from which arises the supreme taste of the nectar of the Dharma, the mark of all wrong conceptions <note>this phrase appears to be misplaced; see the meta note</note>. Beings dwell within the vast blue water of ignorance, stirred up by the wind of improper conceptual thought, and stand before them like reflections of their own karma. When bodhisattvas see them struck at every moment by the suffering of impermanence, and see them as empty of inherent nature, they wish to attain perfectly the state of a Buddha, which is like the destroyer of their suffering of impermanence, the cause from which arises the supreme taste of the nectar of the holy Dharma, marked by the reversal of all wrong conceptions, and whose very nature is to be the friend of all beings.

Bowing deeply to their compassion, whether it focuses on beings, focuses on phenomena, or is without an object, the bodhisattva

<summary>Candrakīrti completes the homage to compassion for beings and turns to the two higher forms of compassion, which focus on phenomena and on no object at all. He uses the image of the moon reflected in rippling water: bodhisattvas see beings as impermanent from moment to moment and empty of inherent nature, and so aspire to buddhahood in order to free them.</summary>
<keywords>Candrakīrti, Madhyamakāvatārabhāṣya, three kinds of compassion, compassion focused on beings, compassion focused on phenomena, objectless compassion, moon in water, reflection, impermanence, emptiness, view of the perishing aggregates, ignorance, nectar of the Dharma, Great Compassion, Blessed Mother</keywords>

<meta>continues from previous page: "...the bodhisattva"</meta>wishes to describe the tenfold division of the bodhisattvas' mind of awakening, and so, with reference to the first mind of awakening, he says:

*The mind of this child of the Victors, which, to free beings,*
*Is under the sway of compassion,*
*Fully dedicated through the prayers of Samantabhadra,*
*And firmly abiding in joy: that is called the first.*

The bodhisattvas' stainless wisdom, embraced by compassion and the rest, receives the name "ground" <term>sa</term> <gloss>bhūmi, stage or level</gloss> when it is divided into parts, because it is the basis of good qualities. It is established as tenfold, divided into the Very Joyful and the others, according to the progressively higher number of qualities, the attainment of supreme power, the excelling in the perfections such as generosity, and the increase of their ripening. In this wisdom itself there is no division made by any distinction of its own nature. As it is said:

*Just as the wise cannot describe*
*Nor see the track of a bird in the sky,*
*So too all the grounds of the Victor's children*
*Cannot be described; how then could they be heard?*

Of these, the bodhisattva ground called the Very Joyful <term>rab tu dga' ba</term> <gloss>Pramuditā</gloss> is the first generation of the mind of the bodhisattvas, and the last, the Cloud of Dharma <term>chos kyi sprin</term> <gloss>Dharmameghā</gloss>, is the tenth.

Here, the bodhisattva sees beings, in the way explained, as lacking inherent nature, and so takes up compassion in its special form. The mind that is under the sway of compassion, fully dedicated through the prayers of the bodhisattva Samantabhadra, named "Very Joyful," and marked by the fruit whose cause is nondual wisdom: this is what is called "the first."

The ten great prayers and the others, the ten countless hundreds of thousands of prayers that a bodhisattva makes on first generating the mind, are all included within the prayers of the bodhisattva Samantabhadra, so that all prayers without exception may be gathered together.

<summary>Candrakīrti introduces the ten bodhisattva grounds, beginning with the first, the Very Joyful, whose mind is ruled by compassion and dedicated through the prayers of Samantabhadra. He explains that the grounds are distinguished by increasing qualities and perfections, not by any difference in the nature of the wisdom itself, which, like a bird's track in the sky, cannot be described.</summary>
<keywords>Candrakīrti, Madhyamakāvatārabhāṣya, ten bhūmis, bodhisattva grounds, Very Joyful, Pramuditā, Cloud of Dharma, Dharmameghā, Samantabhadra, prayers of Samantabhadra, ten great prayers, mind of awakening, compassion, nondual wisdom, perfections, bird's track in the sky</keywords>

<meta>continues from previous page: the reason the prayers are gathered into the prayers of Samantabhadra</meta>the prayers of Samantabhadra are set out as the special prayer.

Just as, in the Vehicle of the Śrāvakas, eight śrāvaka grounds are established according to the distinction between those who are entering and those who abide in the fruits of the path, so in the Great Vehicle there are the ten bodhisattva grounds of the bodhisattvas.

Again, just as the stage in which a śrāvaka produces the factors conducive to penetration is not held to be the stage of one entering the first fruit, so too with the bodhisattva who is about to arise. As it is said in the *Cloud of Jewels Sūtra* <note>the *Ratnamegha Sūtra*</note>: "Abiding immediately before attaining the first ground of the nature of reality, which is practised through the great among great aspiration, is the ground of a bodhisattva in whom the mind of awakening has not yet been generated." And as for one abiding in that moment of practice through aspiration, the same sūtra explains: "Son of good family, it is like this: a universal monarch has passed beyond the condition of a human being but has not attained the condition of a god. In the same way, the bodhisattva has passed far beyond all the grounds of worldly beings, śrāvakas and solitary buddhas, but has not yet attained the ultimate bodhisattva ground." <note>The Tibetan here reads "has attained" (thob pa yin); the sense of the comparison, which parallels the monarch who "has not attained" divine status, suggests a negative was intended.</note>

Further, when one has entered this first ground called the Very Joyful, then:

*From then on, having attained it,*
*He is designated by the very word "bodhisattva."*

One who has attained that mind, in the stage that has passed beyond the ground of ordinary beings in every respect, is to be called only by the word "bodhisattva" and not by any other, because at that time he is a noble one <term>'phags pa</term> <gloss>ārya, one who has directly seen reality</gloss>. As it is said in the *Blessed Mother in Twenty-Five Hundred Lines* <note>a Perfection of Wisdom sūtra</note>: "'Bodhisattva' is a synonym <note>the transcription records two spellings of this word: "bla dgas" and "bla dwags"</note> for a being of realization, one by whom all phenomena are realized and known. How are they known? As unarisen, as not truly arisen, as false; not as foolish ordinary beings have imagined them, and not as foolish ordinary beings have found them. Therefore

<summary>Candrakīrti compares the ten bodhisattva grounds of the Great Vehicle with the eight śrāvaka grounds and explains, citing the *Ratnamegha Sūtra*, that the stage of preparation is not yet the first ground. From the first ground on, one is a noble being and is properly called a "bodhisattva," a term the Perfection of Wisdom explains as "one who realizes all phenomena."</summary>
<keywords>Candrakīrti, Madhyamakāvatārabhāṣya, ten bodhisattva grounds, eight śrāvaka grounds, Very Joyful, Ratnamegha Sūtra, universal monarch, practice through aspiration, factors conducive to penetration, ārya, noble being, ordinary beings, bodhisattva etymology, Perfection of Wisdom in Twenty-Five Hundred Lines, Samantabhadra</keywords>

<meta>continues from previous page: quotation from the Perfection of Wisdom in Twenty-Five Hundred Lines, "Therefore..."</meta>they are called bodhisattvas. Why is that? Awakening is not conceptually constructed. Awakening is not produced. Awakening has no object.

"Suvikrāntavikrāmin <term>rab kyi rtsal gyis rnam par gnon pa</term> <gloss>'He who triumphs with supreme valour,' the bodhisattva to whom this sūtra is addressed</gloss>, the Tathāgata has not found any awakening, because no phenomenon at all is found. It is called awakening because no phenomenon is apprehended. Such is called the awakening of a Buddha; but it is not as it is spoken of.

"Suvikrāntavikrāmin, those who generate the mind toward awakening and think, 'This mind is to be generated toward awakening; there exists an awakening toward which we are to generate the mind,' and so conceive of awakening with conceit, are not to be called bodhisattvas. They are to be called 'beings of arising.' Why? Because they cling to arising, they cling to mind, they cling to awakening," and so on, as the sūtra says.

"Again, awakening is without characteristics: it is free from the nature of characteristics. That by which one realizes in this way is called awakening; and again, it is not as it is spoken of.

"Suvikrāntavikrāmin, one is called a bodhisattva because one realizes these phenomena. Suvikrāntavikrāmin, whoever, while not knowing and not realizing this Dharma, thinks of himself, 'I am a bodhisattva, a bodhisattva,' is far from the bodhisattva ground and far from the qualities of a bodhisattva. Likewise, he deceives the world with its gods, humans and asuras by the name of bodhisattva.

"Suvikrāntavikrāmin, if one became a bodhisattva by mere words, then all beings would become bodhisattvas. Suvikrāntavikrāmin, this is not the work of just anyone; it is the bodhisattva ground," and so on, as is said.

Having attained the mind of awakening as described

<summary>Candrakīrti continues quoting the Perfection of Wisdom sūtra addressed to Suvikrāntavikrāmin. Awakening is unconstructed, unproduced and without object or characteristics; those who cling to awakening as a real thing, or call themselves bodhisattvas in mere words, are far from the bodhisattva ground.</summary>
<keywords>Candrakīrti, Madhyamakāvatārabhāṣya, Suvikrāntavikrāmin, Perfection of Wisdom, awakening, bodhi, bodhisattva, emptiness, nonapprehension, without characteristics, conceit, beings of arising, bodhisattva ground, mind of awakening</keywords>

<meta>continues from previous page</meta>... is, at that stage, not merely designated by the name "bodhisattva" alone. Moreover:

*This one is also born into the family of the Tathāgatas;*
*he has abandoned all three of the fetters.*
*That bodhisattva holds supreme joy,*
*and becomes able to shake a hundred world-systems.*

Because he has passed beyond all the grounds of ordinary beings, of the <term>śrāvakas</term> <gloss>hearers, disciples who seek their own liberation</gloss> and of the <term>pratyekabuddhas</term> <gloss>solitary realizers</gloss>, and because there has arisen in him the path that leads on toward the ground of the Tathāgata called "Universal Light," that bodhisattva is born into the family of the Tathāgatas. At that time, because he sees directly the selflessness of the person, he is also free of the three fetters called the view of the perishing aggregates, doubt, and holding morality and ascetic discipline to be supreme, since these do not arise again. <note>The "view of the perishing aggregates" (Tibetan: 'jig tshogs la lta ba) is the mistaken view that takes the transient body and mind to be a real self.</note> For one who has not seen reality, the view of the perishing aggregates arises from superimposing a self; likewise, through doubt it is possible that he might go off onto some other path, but for this one it is not so.

Because, having entered into certainty, he has obtained the qualities that follow from it, and because he is free of the faults belonging to what opposes the ground, an extraordinary joy not shared with others arises in him. Because of this abundance of great joy, that bodhisattva is also one who holds supreme joy. Since there is a joy that is especially exalted, this ground also receives the name "The Very Joyful." <note>This is the first of the ten bodhisattva grounds, in Sanskrit Pramuditā.</note> He is also able to shake a hundred world-systems.
